https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
A hand-painted placard with “Free Lou!” picked out in blue is propped outside the door of the Just Stop Oil activist Louise Lancaster’s cottage in the picture-perfect village of Grantchester, near Cambridge. She has stuck a wonky “d” to the end of “free”, along with a smiley face.
This month, Lancaster, 58, who was jailed for four years for her part in bringing part of the M25 to a standstill over four days in November 2022, was released, having served nine months of the sentence.
Her children — Tristan, 28, a software engineer, Verity, 26, a midwife, and Theo, 20, a medical student — spoke to me in July last year from this house, just as she was beginning her time at HMP Bronzefield in Surrey. Verity had been looking forward to marrying her fiancé, Jonny, this summer. “Mum is gutted to miss the wedding,” she had said wistfully. “Maybe she’ll get out with a tag and she can wear a long dress.”
At the time, the chances of this happening seemed vanishingly small. But here is Lancaster, sitting in a kitchen full of welcome home cards, her face lightly made up, her hair freshly cut –— a parting gift from a fellow prisoner — and brandishing a black tag around a slender ankle.
She looks well, if thin — she dropped from 60kg to 52kg in Bronzefield, a women’s prison, where she spent the first three months of her sentence — and was often hungry, largely due to the scarcity of vegan protein. “Peanut butter saved me,” she says. It was available to buy in the prison shop. Eventually she was given a vegan pack containing soya milk and yogurt and some seeds. “Everything in prison takes ages,” she says. “The first thing I learned was to lower my expectations almost to a standstill.”
Lancaster’s sentences and those of her four co-defendants Roger Hallam, 57, Daniel Shaw, 40, Lucia Whittaker de Abreu, 37, and Cressida Gethin, 24, were the longest given by a UK judge for non-violent protest. The terms were reduced by a year on appeal in January, making her eligible for a tag that will stay on until September.
She covers her face and laughs when I say I have been trying to think of a tag-concealing mother-of-the-bride outfit. Trouser suit? Maxi dress? The tag looks not unlike a large fitness tracker — you could definitely get away with it at the gym. But being tagged holds no stigma for Lancaster. “It’s a badge of honour,” she says. “I’m at peace with challenging the system. If this is what it takes to show how much I care about the planet and the people on it, then I’m very happy to be wearing it.”
• How Just Stop Oil was policed to extinction
Lancaster did not actually attend the M25 protest in 2022 which, according to the Metropolitan Police, affected more than 700 vehicles, causing work delays and a missed cancer treatment, but she helped organise it, buying climbing equipment and renting an Airbnb where the protesters stayed. She always knew she might go to prison — she had six previous convictions for activism and one five-week prison term — and fully accepted the risk.
“Right at the start of my activism I talked to all my children about how they’d feel if I got arrested,” she explains. “I felt they were able to manage, but you never really know.”
Being separated from them was tougher than she had imagined. “The thing that pressed hardest on me in prison was not being there for my children … If they had a problem, they couldn’t contact me … That’s been really difficult,” she says. Tris and Theo met her as she left prison. “Then Tris did his classic stir-fry with vegetables and tofu — you can’t get a stir-fry in prison.”
Lancaster spent six months at HMP Send, a closed category prison in Surrey where she worked in the gardens for a standard wage of £15 a week and helped other women learn to read. She had her own cell and made some “good friends” with whom she plans to keep in touch.
Most of the women Lancaster met had experienced domestic violence. Some were in for fighting back or for drug offences. “When you spend time with other prisoners you realise how incredibly fortunate you are,” she says. “That really buoys you up. Having a home and a family and good mental health is everything.”
It’s hard to think of a more intensely beautiful English village than Grantchester, where the River Cam shimmers in the spring sunshine.Gas-guzzling 4x4s circle a giant Waitrose but residents here have welcomed her home. “The unfairness of the sentencing really struck a chord with a lot of people,” she says.
In prison, she says she was “love bombed” with letters and cards from supporters. In Grantchester, a vegan potluck supper is being held to welcome her back. “Normally there’d be one vegan item and I’d have brought it myself,” she smiles. It had better be early. Her tag curfew, when she must be at home, runs from 7pm until 7am.
Prosecutors at Lancaster’s trial alleged that the 2022 protest caused economic losses of £765,00 and cost the Met more than £1.1 million. They estimated a total of 50,000 hours of delay was caused, including drivers missing funerals and medical appointments. Lancaster remains unrepentant. “I absolutely stand by the need to carry out those actions at that time, but I also carry with me the people whose lives we disrupted.”
The tough sentences handed out to the “Just Stop Oil five”, whom the judge criticised for their “fanaticism”, were explicitly intended to act as a deterrent. Would Lancaster do it again? “I was asked the same by probation and I don’t know the answer because I don’t know what the future holds,” she says.
For now, she is in a period of reflection. Verity and Jonny have decided to postpone their wedding until next summer so there will be no need for a tag-friendly outfit.
And she has promised her daughter that she will focus her immediate efforts on taking more care of herself. This doesn’t seem an easy thing for her to do — Lancaster still burns with passion for her cause, her eyes still glinting when she discusses it, which is often. “I could just live my nice life, sustaining myself and my family,” she says. “But I have a duty of care as an older person to right some of the wrongs we’ve inflicted on the young.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Roger Hallam, who was jailed for organising disruptive Just Stop Oil protests, was told days before his expected early release that he would not be freed
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
A probation official cited “media ­interest” to prevent the early release from prison of Roger Hallam, an ­environmental activist jailed for ­organising motorway protests.
Last year Hallam, a co-founder of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil, was sentenced to five years but last month that was reduced on appeal by a year.
Hallam, 59, was jailed with four other activists for organising protests that disrupted traffic on the M25 over four days in 2022, when 45 protesters climbed gantries on parts of the motorway, forcing police to stop traffic.
The sentences imposed by the judge, Christopher Hehir, were thought to be the longest ever for peaceful but unlawful protest in ­British history.
Soon after Hallam’s sentence was reduced, he became eligible for home detention curfew and his probation officer told him that he could expect to be released from custody by March 24 this year.
But only days before that date, a prison officer informed Hallam that his ­application had been rejected and that he was being moved from HMP Hollesley Bay, a category D prison near Woodbridge in Suffolk, to a category C prison.
When he queried the decision about his early release, he was told that it was the result of “accommodation and publications”.
Hallam then received an email from a probation officer, Seraphina Evans, saying that she had recommended against his release because of the “increased level of media interest you have accrued since the beginning of your custodial sentence”.
In an email addressed “Dear Julian”, which was Hallam’s first name at birth, Evans said that “in determining whether it is possible to manage the offender safely on early release … the decision-maker must … take into account any relevant information … that would undermine the effectiveness of the risk management plan. For example, where there has been recent behaviour in prison signalling an increased risk of harm on release”.
Evans told him: “I want to assure you that it is not my desire to prevent you from having a voice, nor am I ­setting you up to fail. However, given the media interest you have gathered, I cannot assess [home detention ­curfew] as suitable.”
Hallam’s supporters have said that he had not been told during his time at HMP Hollesley Bay that his general behaviour had been a problem with the authorities. They acknowledged that in November last year, Hallam was reprimanded for recording a podcast called Designing the Revolution but that he stopped immediately and had not been in difficulty with prison officials since.
In a statement, the law firm Bhatt Murphy, which represents Hallam, said that “at a time of serious overcrowding in the prison system, it is extremely disappointing that our client remains in prison”.
Prison officials dispute that Hallam was denied home detention because of media interest and that instead the decision was taken because he had broken prison rules.
